note: Written to be spoken: one sentence or phrase per line; {"beat": s} is a deliberate pause; numbers are phrased the way they are said. `answer` plays after the learner answers a predict step.

lines: The nightly job reads one tebibyte of order events from a local N V M E drive.
The team wants to read it straight from object storage instead.
Before anyone runs it... what is the least time each way could take?
By the end, you'll compute both... and the setting that makes them match.
Let's predict first.
One read from RAM takes about a hundred nanoseconds.
Object storage takes about a hundred milliseconds to send the first byte.
How many RAM reads fit into one object storage wait?
answer: About a million. A hundred milliseconds, divided by a hundred nanoseconds.
That's the gap between one second... and eleven and a half days.
On a straight axis, the RAM read would vanish. So every latency chart from here on is logarithmic... equal steps are equal multiples.

lines: Inside the chip, latency is counted in clock cycles.
Intel's manual gives a Skylake server core four to six cycles to L one, fourteen to L two, and fifty to seventy to L three.
Drepper's rule for main memory, from two thousand seven, is two hundred or more.
At two gigahertz, a cycle is half a nanosecond. So L one is two to three nanoseconds... and D RAM, about a hundred.
Off the chip, the waits jump to microseconds, and then milliseconds.
A random four kilobyte read from an enterprise N V M E drive takes eighty microseconds, says Samsung's datasheet.
A hard disk waits for the platter to turn... four point one six milliseconds on average at seventy two hundred R P M.
Seagate rates it at a hundred and sixty eight random reads a second.
Object storage... a hundred to two hundred milliseconds to the first byte.
The five hundred microsecond round trip is from two thousand nine. Amazon publishes no figure today, so measure yours.
A server with several sockets gives each one its own memory. That's a Numa node.
Memory on another node is slower to reach.
On two thousand seven Opterons, Drepper measured remote reads twenty percent slower.
Linux allocates on the node of the C P U that asks. So a thread that moves to another socket can leave its memory behind.
Measure your own ratio with numa control.
Latency is how long until the first byte.
Bandwidth is how fast the bytes come after that.
They rank the tiers differently.
Object storage is the slowest rung to answer... yet Amazon says one machine can pull up to a hundred gigabits per second from it, given enough requests at once.
A hard disk is slow on both.
Every transfer costs a wait, plus the bytes.
T of n equals alpha plus n over beta.
Read one mebibyte, and the split depends on the tier. A third waiting on N V M E. Nearly two thirds on a hard disk.
On object storage, ninety eight percent... even at one flow's top speed.
Below n equals alpha times beta, a read is mostly waiting. About half a megabyte on this drive. One point seven on the disk.
Here's the lab. Read every number in a one gibibyte array, once in order, once in a random order.
Same count. Same RAM.
How much longer does each random read take?
answer: About twenty times, on this machine.
Memory moves in sixty four byte lines. In order, one line serves eight numbers, and the C P U fetches the next lines before you ask.
At random, each read uses one number of its line... and waits. But the C P U overlaps several waits.
Make each address depend on the last read, and nothing overlaps. A hundred and fifty eight nanoseconds... the whole D RAM wait.
Big O counted all three the same.

lines: One request at a time pays alpha every time.
With k in flight, the waits overlap. So they cost about requests times alpha, divided by k.
One N V M E read takes eighty microseconds alone... twelve thousand five hundred reads a second.
To reach the drive's million a second, you need at least eighty in flight. Samsung measured it with a hundred and twenty eight.
A job can't finish faster than its bytes take at bandwidth beta... or than its waits take with k in flight.
The floor is the larger of the two.
One tebibyte, read in order from N V M E: a hundred and sixty two seconds of bytes, five seconds of waits. Bandwidth bound.
The orders table, page by page at random from a hard disk: twenty nine seconds of bytes, five thousand nine hundred fifty two of waits. Latency bound.
A floor ignores everything else. So a real run is slower.
A full scan is sequential, so its floor is bytes over beta.
The orders table is eight point two gigabytes.
Seven tenths of a second from RAM on one core, measured here. One point two from one N V M E drive. Twenty nine from one hard disk.
If your scan takes a minute on N V M E, the drive isn't the problem. Look for what's spending the other fifty nine seconds.
Back to the problem.
One tebibyte from the N V M E drive: bandwidth bound, a hundred and sixty two seconds.
From object storage, in sixteen mebibyte ranges: sixty five thousand five hundred thirty six requests.
One at a time, the hundred millisecond waits alone take one point eight hours.
With k in flight, they take sixty five hundred fifty four seconds, divided by k. And at k equals forty one, the floor matches the drive.
Each request also streams its sixteen mebibytes. So a real run needs more. Measure the per request rate before you promise it.
Prove it. One of three.
A query goes row by row through an index. Two million random eight kilobyte page reads of orders, one at a time, from one N V M E drive.
What is the floor?
answer: A hundred and sixty seconds. One at a time, every read pays its eighty microsecond wait.
That's a hundred and thirty times the one point two seconds it takes to scan the whole table in order.
With eighty reads in flight, the waits fall to two seconds, and the bytes become the floor. Same reads, a floor sixty six times lower.

lines: Prove it. Two of three.
You copy orders from a local N V M E drive to another instance, over one T C P connection. Not in a cluster placement group.
What is the floor?
answer: Thirteen seconds. A chain runs at its slowest link.
Amazon limits a single flow to five gigabits per second between instances outside a cluster placement group. That's six hundred twenty five megabytes per second, however fast the drive is.
Several connections in parallel can use the instance's full bandwidth instead.

lines: Prove it. Three of three.
The nightly job reads the tebibyte from object storage with eight requests in flight. It takes eighteen minutes.
A teammate says object storage is throttling you.
Is something broken?
answer: With eight in flight, the waits alone take thirteen point seven minutes, and each transfer adds to its wait. So eighteen is about what eight can do.
The job sends eighty requests a second, against at least fifty five hundred allowed. It's latency bound. Raise k... or use fewer, larger ranges.
